title: useRef: mutable values & DOM refs
objectives: Explain that useRef returns the same mutable box every render and writing .current never re-renders
Choose a ref or state for a value by asking whether a change to it should update the screen
Spot a ref read or written during render, and move it into an event handler or effect
Predict that a DOM ref is null during the first render and is set only after React commits
Write a DOM ref that moves focus after an action, where `autoFocus` (focus on mount) can't reach

sources.title: React docs: Referencing Values with Refs
React docs: Manipulating the DOM with Refs

questions.prompt: What does useRef(0) return, and what happens when you write to it?

options.text: A stable { current: 0 } object; writing ref.current mutates it without triggering a re-render
The number 0; reassigning it schedules a re-render like state
A [value, setValue] pair just like useState
A fresh object on every render, so .current resets to 0 each time

questions.explanation: useRef returns the SAME mutable object { current } on every render. Writing ref.current changes it silently — React is not notified, so nothing re-renders. That silence is the feature: refs hold values the UI doesn't need to react to.

questions.prompt: You need a value that persists across renders. When should it be a ref instead of state?

options.text: When changing the value should NOT cause the component to re-render (it isn't shown or read during render)
Always — refs are faster than state, so prefer them
Only when the value is a primitive; objects must use state
Only for values defined outside the component

questions.explanation: Refs and state both survive re-renders. The deciding question is whether a change should update the screen. If the value is displayed or drives what's displayed, use state (it re-renders). If it's bookkeeping the render never reads — a timer id, a previous value, a flag — use a ref (it stays silent).

questions.prompt: You attach a ref to an `<input>` to call `.focus()`. Where is it safe to read `inputRef.current`?

options.text: In an effect or an event handler — after React has committed the DOM
Directly in the render body, right after useRef
Anywhere — a DOM ref is never null once declared
In the render body, as long as you check `if (inputRef.current)` first

questions.explanation: During the first render the DOM node doesn't exist yet, so inputRef.current is null; during later renders the DOM hasn't been updated yet. React sets the ref during commit. Read it in an effect (runs after commit) or an event handler (runs when the user interacts). A null check in the render body avoids the crash but not the problem: the render still reads a value React doesn't track, so what it shows depends on when it happened to render.

questions.prompt: Which of these focus jobs needs a DOM ref, because `autoFocus` can't do it?

options.text: Putting focus back in the search box after the user clicks **Clear** (the box is already on screen)
Focusing the search box when the page first shows it
Focusing the edit field that appears when the user clicks **Edit** (it mounts at that moment)
None of them — React can't focus an element without a ref

questions.explanation: `<input autoFocus>` tells React to focus the element when it **mounts**. That covers the first-load box and, less obviously, the edit field: it mounts when Edit is clicked, so `autoFocus` fires right then. The Clear case is different: the input is already mounted, so moving focus in response to an action means calling `.focus()` on the real node — `inputRef.current.focus()` in the click handler.

questions.prompt: A component shows how often it has rendered with `renders.current += 1` in its body. In development under StrictMode (React 19.2, which this course runs), the very first mount already shows **2**. Why?

options.text: StrictMode calls the component body twice in development to catch impure rendering, and writing a ref during render is impure
useRef creates a new box on each call, so the count is reset and re-added
React always renders a component twice on mount, in production too
StrictMode re-ran the component's effects, and effects re-render the component

questions.explanation: StrictMode calls the component body twice in development to surface impure rendering, and `renders.current += 1` is a write during render — react.dev says not to write or read `ref.current` while rendering (lazy initialization is the one exception). In React 19.2 the second call reuses the first call's ref, so both increments land in the same box and the first mount reads 2; if each call got a fresh box, you would see 1. Production calls the body once and the same code shows 1 — the number tracks how React chose to call the component, not anything real. Write refs in event handlers or effects, and use the React DevTools Profiler to see renders. StrictMode's extra effect run re-runs effects, not the component body, so it adds nothing to this count.

prompts.prompt: Clicking **Reply** should put the cursor in the comment box: declare a ref, attach it, then focus it from the click handler.
prompts.explanation: useRef(null) makes the box, the `ref={boxRef}` attribute tells React to put the `<textarea>` DOM node into it at commit, and by the time the user can click Reply, `boxRef.current` is that node — so the handler can call `.focus()`. `autoFocus` couldn't do this: the textarea is already mounted when the click happens.

prompts.prompt: Store an interval id without causing a re-render, then read it back to clear it.
prompts.explanation: The interval id is plumbing the UI never renders, so it belongs in a ref. Writing id.current is silent (no re-render), and you can read the same .current back later to clear the interval.

snippets.question: You click the button five times. What number does the label show?
snippets.explanation: count.current really does climb to 5 in memory — but mutating a ref never tells React to re-render, so the button never repaints. It still shows the value from the last render: 0. The bug is reading `count.current` during render: if anything else re-rendered the component, the label would jump straight to 5. A value the screen shows belongs in state.

snippets.question: What does the console.log print during the very first render?
snippets.explanation: React only assigns inputRef.current during commit, after the render has returned the `<input>`. During the first render the node doesn't exist yet, so the ref still holds its initial value, null. (In development, StrictMode calls the component twice; both calls print null.) Read DOM refs in effects or handlers, not the render body.
